blocks.text: Rewritten copy for the 4-step paywall lead-in: new headline, subline and value props on the intro screen, new title copy plus a second testimonial on the social proof screen, and a new headline and bullets on the pricing screen (a) vs the existing copy (b)

Mixpanel, Aurie Mobile, 2026-08-04 -> 2026-08-25 (real launch window; the row's Start Date 2026-07-27 is the catalog registration date). Denominator N = AI Sign Up Login unique users. a = new copy, b = control. Note the arm imbalance (1829 vs 1705, +7.3%); every rate below is per-user so the imbalance does not drive it.

Exposure quality — the property is not attached at sign-up, so no over-stamping; the raw cut is trustworthy.

Internal/comped screen: applied to the heavy tail only — the top 1% of each arm by session count (38 unique UIDs, min 33 sessions). Both nets ran clean (cohort + per-subscription code scan, complete=true) and 0 were internal, so the tail is organic. The screen was NOT applied to the full ~3,000-user population, so the arm denominators below are unscreened aggregates.

Variant a won on Aurie's primary metric. Avg Sessions per User is up 14.4%, and unlike the close-button tests this survives trimming — +12.6% after dropping the top 1% of users and +9.1% with sessions capped at 20 — so it is broad-based across the middle and upper distribution rather than a few heavy accounts. The heavy tail is organic (0 of 38 top-1% accounts internal). Monetization is genuinely tied (Purchased +2.2%, Paid +1.4%), and session reach is identical at 64.5%, so the copy is not pulling in more people — it is making the people it reaches come back more. DISAGREEMENT: the team read this as 'results are tied' and shipped variant a on 2026-08-25 for the better user experience, treating it as a no-cost UX change. That undersells it. Judged on the metric Aurie declares primary, this is the only one of the four experiments in the batch that actually won, and the mechanism is worth reusing: honest value framing bought engagement that paywall friction could not.

- Port the winning lead-in copy pattern to the other Aurie paywall surfaces and re-measure Avg Sessions per User, since that is where the gain landed. Primary metric: Avg Sessions per User.
- Decompose the win: the variant changed three screens at once (intro copy, second testimonial, pricing bullets). Test the second testimonial alone against the copy rewrite alone to find which half carries the +9-13%. Primary metric: Avg Sessions per User.
- Re-run with balanced arms and a pre-registered engagement primary to confirm the effect at 95%; the current read is a robust point estimate but the batch was never powered for an engagement call. Primary metric: Avg Sessions per User.
- Check whether the engagement lift converts on a longer horizon than the 20-day window allowed — flat Paid at day 20 with +14% sessions is the shape that turns into paid later. Primary metric: Day-60 Paid Subscription Rate.
remove the Yearly discount copy Card of paywall
Independently re-cut from Mixpanel on 2026-08-08 (project 963821, all-country, user-level assignment over 7/30-8/8). The two arms are flat — no metric separates them.

The -28.4% @95.0% Trial Start figure recorded on the experiment server is a US-only sub-cut at 37 vs 49 trials — below the team's own >=50-conversions-per-arm bar. #abtest-monitoring retracted it on 2026-08-08: -28.4% @95.0% became -20.6% @84.6% (US) and -1.4% @9.9% all-country, logged as "classic noise resolving". Our independent pull reproduces the all-country figure exactly (-1.4%, 9.5% confidence).

Exposure quality. Experiment: removeYearlyDiscountCopy is a user-profile property, not an event super-property — an event-level cut returns 1 user in total, so there is no over-stamping diluting the raw cut. Assigned 596 vs N 548: a 48-user gap (8.1%), balanced across arms (a 20 / b 28), consistent with internal/QA accounts plus assignments too recent for events to land. Internal/comped screening was not applied (aggregate-only run, no per-user JQL pass), so the population above is unscreened.

Removing the "50% off" copy from the yearly plan card changed nothing measurable. At 276 vs 272 registrations and 90 vs 90 trial starts, the primary metric lands at -1.4% with 9.5% confidence — the arms are indistinguishable on trial start, paid conversion and trial cancellation alike. The copy was suspected of being misleading rather than of carrying conversion weight (PROD-3587), and this result is consistent with it carrying none: the claim can be corrected or dropped on accuracy grounds without paying for it at the paywall.

Verdict recorded as Inconclusive, not Lost. The formal AuraBot end-note on 2026-08-07 closed this as *Experiment Lost — winner b (control)*, and the server result field still carries the -28.4% headline. That headline did not survive one more day of data. Our read is that the experiment reached an adequate sample on its primary (90 conversions per arm, above the 50/arm bar) and detected no effect — a genuine null, not a loss for variant a. Shipping control was still the right call; there was simply no evidence against the treatment.

Methodology note worth carrying forward. The signal that drove the kill was produced by event-level assignment on a mobile-only slice (-32.9% @95.9% on 8/6), which is survivorship-biased; re-pulling with the canonical user-level property on 8/7 weakened it, and it decayed to non-significance by 8/8. The team caught this in flight, but only after a stakeholder pushed back on the number. Two standing hazards this run illustrates: a US-only cut disagreeing with the matched all-country cut (an open question raised across three concurrent experiments), and a decision taken at Day 8 against a stated 14-day minimum runtime.

Ship the accurate discount, don't just delete the claim. showRealYearlyDiscount (PROD-4328) already computes the true saving against the 6-month plan. Hypothesis: a credible, correct percentage beats both the inflated "50% off" and no badge at all. Primary metric: Trial Start Rate. This experiment shows the removal is free, so the upside now sits entirely in the replacement.

Resolve the canonical Aura population before the next paywall test. A prerequisite rather than a product experiment: US-only vs all-country flipped the read on three concurrent experiments (paywallOnStart, removeYearlyDiscountCopy, auraPaywallAddFAQs), sometimes in opposite directions. Fix the denominator once and every subsequent paywall readout gets cheaper and more trustworthy.

Test the yearly card's value framing, not its badge. Copy removal was a null, which suggests the badge is not what the user is reading. Hypothesis: restating the yearly plan as a per-month equivalent ("$5.83/month, billed yearly") moves plan selection more than any discount claim. Primary metric: yearly-plan share of Trial Start.

Pre-register a stopping rule. This ran 8 of a planned 14 days and was called on a sub-cut that later retracted. Hypothesis: committing the population, primary metric and minimum conversions per arm before launch reduces retracted calls. Measure on process, not users: count of flagged-then-retracted signals per quarter.

Shows CTA Button at bottom of paywall , a - show cta button at bottom , b - normal flow

Exposure quality: cannot be measured for this experiment.

The Experiment: auraPaywallCTAPosition property exists only as a USER profile
property - it is never stamped on events. An event-level breakdown returns 100%
undefined (1,040 of 1,041 sign-up-login events carry no variant). So the
over-stamping check cannot be run, and there is no way to isolate the users who
actually rendered the paywall from the users merely assigned at registration.

Consequence: every rate above is computed over ALL assigned registrants, not over
an exposed cohort. Dilution is symmetric across arms, so the DIRECTION of the
result is safe; the true effect on users who saw the paywall is larger in absolute
terms than the numbers above, not smaller.

Assigned vs N gap: 1,121 assigned vs 1,039 signed in (82 users, 7.3%). 8 are
internal accounts; the rest were assigned but fired no sign-up-login in the window.

Moving the Aura paywall's subscribe CTA to the very bottom cost paid conversion with no upside on any other metric. Variant a lost 33.0% of Paid Rate against control (5.73% vs 8.54%, ~92% confidence) and 28.2% of trial-to-paid conversion. Trial starts were down 6.7% and trial cancellations up 3.9%, neither significant - so the damage is concentrated exactly where the layout change acts: users reached the plan cards but converted to paid less often once the CTA stopped sitting with them. Verdict Lost; control (b) shipped.

The decisive finding is that Aura had already run this test and it had already lost. paywallCTAPosition ended 2026-06-17 on AuraConsumerApp with the same treatment concept and the same outcome - variant a (sticky bottom CTA) turned off 6/15 for "paid starts way lower", variant c (dual CTA) turned off 6/17 at a Paid Subscription Rate 64% below control (6.38% vs 17.54%). The request for this experiment (ENGMOB-1908) was filed 2026-06-22, five days after that conclusion, and its stated rationale was "it follows a massive win seen on Aurie" - the Aurie prior was used while Aura's own contradicting result from the previous week was not. Two experiment cycles were spent re-learning the same thing.

The transferable learning is about priors, not about CTAs: an Aurie paywall win is not evidence for Aura. Aurie is a conversation product whose paywall sits inside an engagement loop; Aura is a content product whose paywall is a purchase decision at the plan cards. CTA placement is precisely the kind of layout variable whose effect depends on that surrounding funnel, and it has now reversed sign across the two apps twice. Before porting an Aurie paywall win to Aura, check the Aura catalog for the same treatment first.

Caveat on magnitude: paid counts are modest (30 vs 44), and the same channel has documented rate lifts on thin windows evaporating on matured data (fourStepPaywallAura went from +55% Paid Starts to +1.4% $/reg once matured). The direction here is well-supported and consistent with the June result; the -33% point estimate should not be quoted as a precise effect size.

Stop porting Aurie paywall layout wins to Aura without an Aura-side prior check. Not an experiment - a process change. Add a step to experiment intake that greps the Aura experiment catalog for the same treatment before a card is written. This experiment and paywallCTAPosition would both have been caught by it.

Test CTA proximity rather than CTA position. Hypothesis: paid conversion depends on the CTA being visible at the moment the user finishes comparing plans, not on where it sits in the page. Variants: a = CTA pinned directly beneath the plan cards (moves up, not down), b = control. Primary metric: Trial -> Paid. This is the opposite direction to what just lost and is the untested half of the hypothesis space.

Investigate why Aurie's CTA-at-bottom win does not transfer. Hypothesis: the two paywalls differ in scroll depth and in how much content sits between the plan cards and the CTA. A read-only teardown comparing the two surfaces (scroll length, elements between plans and CTA, time-to-CTA-visible) would say whether the Aurie win was about position at all, or about something else that came with it.

Re-test on the exposed cohort once the experiment property is event-stamped. This experiment could not measure exposure at all. Stamping Experiment: <name> at paywall render would let future paywall tests compute rates over users who actually saw the surface, which is where the effect is. Worth doing before the next paywall experiment, not after.

Yearly subscription price test on Aura mobile: a: $79.99/year, b: control, c: $89.99/year
Inconclusive — the intended control price was never served on iOS, so the headline contrast is unmeasurable. Numbers below are recorded for the audit trail, not as a verdict.

The experiment cannot be read, and that is the finding. Arm b had no dedicated control SKU: it fell through to the permanent iOS yearly price, which a prior won experiment (appleNewUpdatedPriceForNewUsers, removed in Aura#6504) had already moved to $79.99 — the same price as arm a. PROD-4638 root-caused this on 2026-08-18 and the $69.99 restore only shipped in v3.19.147/148 on 2026-08-20, the day before the experiment was ended, so effectively the entire 22-day run served $79.99 / $79.99 / $89.99 rather than the intended $69.99 / $79.99 / $89.99. The $69.99 label came from the Android fallback path only.

Taken at face value the numbers do not support the recorded "Lost" either. On the all-country cut, Paid Rate over N is dead flat (9.21% / 9.15% / 9.13%) and paid-per-trial-start is higher in both treatments than in control; the only consistent signal is a lower Trial Start Rate in both (a -15.7%, c -2.2%), which is directionally what a price rise should do but is contaminated by the same defect. Yawar independently spotted the tell: a at $79.99 started fewer trials than c at $89.99, which is not how price behaves, so a's deficit is likely noise. Two further confounds remain even after the SKU fix: most Aura mobile users are routed to a webview and pay via Stripe, so the native IAP arm may not describe what an assigned user was actually charged, and webYearlyPricing was running concurrently on web.

Verdict recorded as Inconclusive rather than Lost. The pricing question is untested, not answered — treating this as "the price rise lost" would retire a live revenue hypothesis on a broken measurement. Note also that no exposure-time attribution is possible here: the variant lives on the user profile rather than as an event super-property, so an over-stamping check is unverifiable and only ~50% of assigned users ever reached the paywall.
Four next steps, ordered — the first two split the question the broken run conflated:

Clean two-arm re-run ($79.99 vs $89.99, explicit control SKU) — the contrast the current data actually served. Hypothesis: at the already-shipped $79.99 baseline, a further rise to $89.99 loses more trial starts than it gains in revenue per payer. Primary metric: Trial Start Rate, with paid-per-trial-start as the confirmation. Blocked on PROD-4638 landing.

Re-test the original question ($69.99 vs $79.99) separately, since the permanent price is now $79.99 on iOS and $69.99 on Android — the platforms have silently diverged. Hypothesis: the $10 step is invisible to conversion. Primary metric: Trial Start Rate, cut by platform.

Segment any pricing re-run by payment rail (native IAP vs webview/Stripe). Hypothesis: a native price arm moves nothing for the webview-routed majority, which would explain the flat revenue-per-payer Steve flagged on 2026-08-12. Primary metric: Paid Rate split by Paywall Type.

Guardrail, not an experiment: add the PROD-4638 acceptance check so removing a won experiment cannot silently repoint a live experiment's control price. This run cost 22 days of mobile paywall traffic.

Replace Continue button for no question replies with text input
Post-rollout confirmation (Alyssa Luboff, 2026-07-13 -- Conversation traces + Mixpanel, ~2 weeks before [Jun 13-27] vs after [Jun 29-Jul 13], full rollout to 100% on 2026-06-28):
Synthetic "Continue" turns: ~2% of text turns -> 0% (mechanism fully off)
Empty/blank replies (text QP): 0 -> 0 -- eliminates the exact failure the button was causing
Button-induced guardrail loops: none remain; residual guardrail responses are correct replies to typed messages

Of 42 post-rollout no-question moments (the old button trigger spot): 67% replied naturally, 14% gave a short reply (81% kept talking), only 10% didn't reply/exited, and a residual 10% still typed "continue" (likely stale app versions) but all closed cleanly
Completion rate 46.5% -> 50.1%; cancellation rate 41.1% -> 33.2%; ratings and back-button taps flat -- no harm to engagement

The original AB read was underpowered (tens of sessions per arm) and called a tie by the team, who shipped variant a on UX preference. A stronger post-rollout before/after analysis (2026-07-13) confirms it was the right call: the mechanism this experiment targeted -- the mid-conversation Continue button, which drove ~2/3 of QP guardrail hand-offs and 95% of empty responses per the original 90-day problem analysis -- was fully eliminated after 100% rollout, with zero blank replies and zero button-induced guardrail loops. Users overwhelmingly (81%) replied naturally where the button used to appear. No harm to engagement -- completion rate and cancellation rate both moved favorably. Net: benefit, no harm -- treat as a win despite the inconclusive initial AB read, since that read measured the wrong thing (raw session counts on tiny N) rather than the actual failure modes this change was designed to fix.
Investigate 3 blank replies that appeared in voice QP on 2026-06-30 (voice never had a Continue button, so unrelated to this change -- flagged separately by Alyssa Luboff)

If a measured engagement-lift claim is needed later, re-run with a properly powered cohort -- the completion/cancellation deltas above are directional (before/after, not a controlled AB) and shouldn't be cited as a measured lift on their own

The window predates the current Aura event taxonomy, so the metered event names
('Sign up login', 'Subscription Trial Started') do not match what was being emitted
for most of it. Zero in both arms over 514 days is an instrumentation gap, not
user behaviour.

The experiment also carries no end-note in #data-experiment and an empty result
on the experiment server - the only one of the 31 with neither.

Nothing was learned, and nothing can be recovered.

This ran 514 days from 2023-09-22 to 2025-02-17 - the longest window in the
catalogue by a factor of ten - and returns zero sign-ups and zero trials in both
arms. The window predates the current event taxonomy, so the events that would
carry the answer were never emitted under the names that would find them. Eight
paid events across both arms is all that is attributed.

Spec — not launched. Owner: Daniel. Flip Status to Running and fill Start/End Date on launch day.
Why this is the biggest lever on the board
870 annual subscribers a month hit a failed renewal. None of them are contacted. The 9% that come back are recovered entirely by Stripe Smart Retries.
This is a first-contact lever, not an optimization lever. There is no incumbent email to beat.
What the archive says — read before arguing about the offer
This problem has been attacked four times from the wrong angle and lost every time:
Two things fall out of that table.

One: the surface was wrong, not the intervention. Every loss above put the message somewhere the user had to already be in the app to see it. A user whose card silently declined has no reason to open Aura that week. Email is the one channel that reaches them without requiring the behaviour we are trying to restore — and it is the one channel never tried on this cohort. Daniel's read is right, and the archive supports it rather than undercutting it.

Two: discounts have lost here twice. fpRenewalChurn and pushTrialCancelled both put money on the table and both lost. That is the single strongest reason the offer arm below carries a plan switch at list price rather than a discount.

One more prior worth pulling forward: fpRenewalChurn2 Won in Dec 2023, and its win was not in conversion — trial and paid rates were flat (19.5% vs 19.3% on N≈9k/arm). The recorded API note is "a Lower refunds 24%". A renewal intervention at Aura has already been shown to pay off through refunds rather than through recovery rate. That shapes the metric design below, and it is the whole reason pre-dunning gets measured on net revenue.
Three arms, assigned at customer level, so a customer who fails twice in the window stays in the arm they were first assigned to.

Why A exists at all. Without it, the whole first-contact lift — which will be most of the lift — lands on the offer arm and gets written up as "the downgrade offer works." Then the offer ships, the discount precedent gets set, and nobody knows whether a plain card-update email would have delivered 90% of it for free. A is the arm that makes the readout mean something.

Why email 1 is identical in A and B. Introducing the offer at first contact downgrades people who would simply have updated an expired card — you would be paying for recoveries you were getting anyway. Holding the offer until email 2 lets the easy fixes resolve at full price and aims the offer at the residual. The cost is that offer timing becomes a confound with offer presence; that is deliberate, and offer-at-day-0 is the natural follow-up test once the offer itself is proven.

Why 40/40/20 rather than thirds. The holdout is the expensive arm — every user in it is a user we knowingly do not try to recover, at roughly $924/mo in forgone recovery at 20%. Shrinking it to 20% cuts that cost while still powering the headline comparison faster than equal allocation would, because the pooled A+B group grows.
Unit: Stripe customer ID, hashed and bucketed at first invoice.payment_failed on an annual subscription. Sticky for 180 days.
In scope: Aura annual subscriptions billed through Stripe, first failure of the renewal invoice.

Out of scope: App Store / Play Store billing (different dunning mechanics entirely — worth its own spec), monthly plans, subscriptions already in a cancellation flow, anyone who cancelled voluntarily before the renewal date.
Stratify on decline-code family (see pre-work) so an unlucky split on expired_card vs insufficient_funds does not swamp a 3-point effect.
Cadence, pinned to the Smart Retries window

Smart Retries spreads up to four ML-timed attempts over roughly three weeks. The emails ride alongside it rather than running on their own clock, so the user is never told "your payment failed" on a day Stripe has already succeeded.
Suppression: any send is cancelled on invoice.paid, customer.subscription.deleted, or a successful plan switch. Cap one email per day per customer across all Aura streams during the window.
The offer — both variants designed, one ships first

Daniel asked for both a discounted annual and a monthly downgrade. Both are specified below. Only one can be in Arm B without destroying the power budget (a fourth arm pushes the A-vs-B read past eight months), so one ships in Test 1 and the other becomes the Test 2 challenger.
Recommendation: monthly downgrade at list price ships first

It matches the failure mode. An $89 single charge failing on a thin card is a charge-size problem. A 30%-off annual is still a $62 lump sum landing on the same card. Monthly at list is the only offer that changes the shape of the ask rather than just its size.

Aura has lost on discounts twice at exactly this moment (fpRenewalChurn, pushTrialCancelled). Leading with a discount means the likely outcome is another loss that also costs margin and sets a precedent that is hard to walk back once support starts quoting it.

Aura already sells monthly and it already won (addMonthlyPackagePaywall, Won). The SKU exists, the price is public, and the plan switch runs through the Stripe Customer Portal with no new billing surface to build.

The counter-case, stated fairly: if the decline-code distribution comes back dominated by expired_card, then neither offer is the lever — the answer is a better card-update path and the Account Updater work in the pre-work section — and the monthly offer will look flat for the right reason. Run the decline-code pull before launch so this is a known quantity rather than a post-hoc explanation.

The trap: recovery rate and recovery revenue diverge the moment you offer a cheaper plan. Arm B can beat Arm A on recovery rate and still lose money. Break-even depends on how long a recovered monthly subscriber survives.
Assuming Arm A recovers 14%, and Arm B recovers the same population as 9% at annual + 8% switching to monthly:

We already have this number. Median tenure of Aura's existing monthly cohort is a query, not an assumption — pull it before launch and write the break-even threshold into this doc. If existing monthly subs survive 6+ months, the offer is comfortably accretive at any of these prices. If they survive 3, it is a revenue-negative recovery machine and the arm should be reconsidered.
Same shift assumptions (14% plain; offer arm = 9% at full price + 8% at a discount). Maximum discount depth before year-1 revenue falls below Arm A:

The first row is the pessimistic case and the one to design against: cap any discount at 30%, which leaves a margin of safety. Frame it as a one-time credit ("$25 off this year's renewal"), not a rate cut — a dollar amount doesn't reset the customer's reference price the way a percentage does, and it doesn't renew.
Third option worth its own slot later

Neither offer addresses the user who genuinely cannot pay right now. subscriptionPauseInCancellation is already running on the cancellation flow; a defer-30-days option in the dunning sequence is the cheapest possible save — no discount, no plan change, no revenue loss, just a later charge date. Worth queuing as Test 3.
Primary: net recovered revenue per 1,000 failed invoices, measured at day 60.

Not recovery rate. Recovery rate is the metric that makes Arm B look like a winner while it quietly trades $88.50 annual subs for $12.99 monthly ones. Net recovered revenue is defined as: renewal revenue collected + 12-month contracted value of any plan switch at its actual price, minus refunds, minus chargebacks. Day 60 because Smart Retries runs ~21 days and the offer window and refund window need to close before the number is stable.
Report recovery rate as the headline secondary — it is the number everyone will ask for, and the gap between it and net revenue is the most interesting thing this test will produce.
Recovery rate (any successful payment within 60 days)
Split of recoveries: full annual / switched to monthly / recovered after switch
Email funnel per step: delivered, open, click, card updated, paid
Time to recovery (which email in the sequence does the work)
Downstream: 90-day retention of recovered subs, by arm and by recovery path
That last one matters: the offer email tells a lapsed user their subscription exists. Some of them will use that information to cancel outright. Watch it.

One consent note. The plain sequence is transactional — a billing notice for a live contract. The offer block arguably makes Arm B promotional. Get this classified before launch: if it has to go out under marketing consent, Arm B's addressable population shrinks and the arms are no longer comparable. Most billing-adjacent counsel will land on "transactional with an embedded service option," but confirm rather than assume.
Run 16 weeks, fixed horizon, with one futility check at week 7.

The holdout answer lands at week 7. Do not ship on it and kill the test — the offer question is the one that determines whether a discount precedent enters Aura's playbook, and it needs the full run. What week 7 does buy: if pooled email is not beating the holdout by then, stop, because nothing downstream matters.
Accept +4pp as the B-vs-A MDE. Chasing +3pp costs another twelve weeks for a difference that would not change the decision.

Holdout cost: 174 users/mo × 6pp × $88.50 ≈ $924/mo forgone, roughly $3.4k over the 16-week run. That is the price of knowing whether the offer or the contact did the work, and it is cheap against a $55k/yr decision. Take it to whoever needs to sign off on it explicitly rather than burying it.
Peeking: one interim look at week 7, pre-registered. No other peeks. If someone wants a continuous readout, use a sequential boundary (O'Brien-Fleming) and say so here before launch, not after.
Decision rules — write these down before you look at data

Stripe's built-in failed-payment emails are a single template with no variant support and no arbitrary CTA — they cannot run three arms, and they cannot carry a plan-switch link. Given that 870 users/mo are currently uncontacted, they are presumably switched off today. So:
Keep Smart Retries as the retry engine. Do not change the retry schedule during the test; it is a shared confound across all three arms and must stay frozen.
Leave Stripe's native emails off. Turning them on for some arms and not others introduces a second sender and a second template.
Trigger sends off invoice.payment_failed webhooks into Iterable. Aura already runs Iterable (iterableChurnPrevention, iterableContentvsSale, and others), so this is wiring, not a new vendor.
Arm A CTA → invoice.hosted_invoice_url. Stripe-hosted, no build, updates the card and charges in one step.

Arm B CTA → Stripe Customer Portal with plan switching enabled, deep-linked to the monthly SKU. Also no custom billing surface. Confirm proration behaviour on a switch from a failed annual invoice — the unpaid invoice should be voided, not prorated into the new plan.
Webhook payload must carry: customer ID, arm assignment, invoice ID, amount, decline code, attempt number, last4, card brand, card expiry.
If Iterable cannot be triggered off Stripe webhooks without engineering work, that is the critical-path blocker and it should be sized before anything else in this doc gets scheduled.
Pre-work — three pulls, all cheap, all before launch

Decline-code distribution across the 870. Group into expired_card / insufficient_funds / do_not_honor / generic_decline / other. This determines whether the offer hypothesis is even live, and it is the stratification variable. If expired_card dominates, say so out loud now rather than discovering it in the readout.
Median tenure and 12-month revenue of Aura's existing monthly cohort. Turns the break-even table above from a sensitivity analysis into a threshold.

fpRenewalChurn2's actual mechanics. It Won in Dec 2023 on a 24% refund reduction and the page has no record of what was tested. Someone knows. Finding out may mean this test is partly re-running something that already shipped — worth twenty minutes to check.

And one build that is not an experiment: Stripe Card Account Updater plus network tokenization. If expired_card is a meaningful share of the 870, this recovers subscriptions with no email, no offer and no user action at all. It may be worth more than everything in this doc. It is not an A/B test, it is a configuration change — but do not ship it mid-test, because it changes the denominator.

Deliberately unadorned. No usage recap, no personalization beyond name and card, no social proof. Arm A's job is to isolate contact; every extra ingredient contaminates that. Usage personalization is a good idea and belongs in a later test, not this one.

Every subject line names the problem in the first four words. Dunning emails are not the place for curiosity gaps; a user who doesn't open this loses their subscription.
No exclamation marks, no "Oops!", no apology. The tone is a bank notice written by someone who likes you.
"It's usually something simple" in E1 is doing real work: it removes the implication that the user's card was rejected for lack of funds, which is the reading that makes people ignore the email.
E5 in Arm A explicitly offers the exit. Counterintuitive, but it is the line that keeps complaint rate down, and complaint rate on this cohort is a deliverability risk for every other Aura email.
{{grace_end_date}} must be the real date the subscription cancels in Stripe. If the email says one date and Stripe does another, that is a support and chargeback problem, not a copy problem.
Designed here so the program is complete, but not launched alongside the dunning test. It gets its own row in this database when it's scheduled.

A T-7 renewal notice changes who lands in dunning at all — fewer expired cards, fewer surprise charges, and a different mix of decline reasons among those who still fail. Running both at once means the dunning test's denominator shifts underneath it mid-flight. Running pre-dunning first means waiting four months for the bigger lever. So: dunning first, pre-dunning starts the week the dunning test closes, and the dunning baseline gets re-measured afterwards.
The thing that makes this test different

A renewal reminder can lose money by working. It tells a user who forgot they subscribed that they subscribed. Some of them cancel. The upside is quieter: fewer failed charges, fewer refund requests, fewer chargebacks.

We have evidence for exactly this shape at Aura. fpRenewalChurn2 Won in Dec 2023 with trial and paid rates essentially flat (19.5% vs 19.3%, N≈9k/arm) — the recorded win was "a Lower refunds 24%". A renewal intervention here has already paid off through refunds rather than conversion.

So the primary metric is net revenue retained per 1,000 upcoming renewals at day 45 post-renewal — renewal revenue collected, minus refunds, minus chargebacks. Involuntary failure rate is a secondary. Anyone who proposes judging this on failure rate alone is measuring the half of the effect that flatters the test.
B is the arm with a real mechanism: a user whose card expires in nineteen days cannot act on information nobody gives them. A is the compliance-grade floor.

Highest-yield segment: subscribers whose card on file expires before the renewal date. Pre-register it. It is small, the effect there should be large, and it is the segment that justifies the build even if the overall read is flat.
Compliance — check before assuming the holdout is legal

Advance renewal notice for annual auto-renewals is required or effectively required in several jurisdictions — California's Automatic Renewal Law is the one most likely to bind Aura given the subscriber base, and the federal negative-option landscape has been in flux. This is a question for counsel, not for this doc. Two consequences if notice turns out to be mandatory:
Arm C is not available and the test becomes A vs B, which is fine — it is also the more interesting comparison.
The T-7 notice ships regardless of what the test says, and the test is only choosing between two versions of a thing you have to send anyway.
Worth resolving early: it changes whether this is a growth experiment or a compliance build with an experiment attached.

Nothing here is decision-grade, and nothing here is evidence against $159.99. Attach was directionally up (14.0% vs 11.1%, +2.9pp at ~64% confidence on n = 8 vs 6) and booked revenue per trial start was up +$6.40 (+7.2%) once the crossed yearly test is held constant — but on 14 family trial starts in total, one or two sales either way swings the whole delta. Read it as no damage from the higher price, not as a lift.

The finding that outranks the experiment: mobile family plan sales are at zero, and nobody owns turning the surface back on. With familyPlanWebviewUpsell (PROD-3624) off, ~$5.2k/mo of mobile family gross is going to $0 — on the conservative paid-event sizing, and the success-event volume implies more. That is a live cash leak, independent of any pricing question, and it was found by someone asking why a counter had stopped rather than by anything monitoring it.

The generalisable lesson is about dependency, not pricing. A live experiment silently became unreadable because a *different* experiment's variant assignment removed the surface its primary metric depended on. Nothing in the experiment server or the monitor flagged the coupling. The second-order lesson is the crossing: two concurrent price tests over the same traffic made the all-in per-registration cut unreadable and left the arms imbalanced on the other test's dimension — the same trap webYearlyPricing2 set on web.

Sizing context for whoever picks this up: mobile is only ~8% of family volume. Repricing all mobile family to $159.99 is worth ~+$15.5k/yr net at flat attach, ~+$25.7k/yr if the attach edge is real, and break-even tolerates losing 25% of family sales. The far bigger lever is the 283 Stripe family subscriptions still renewing at $129.99 (~$36.8k/mo) — moving those to $159.99 is ~+$8.5k/mo (~+$102k/yr) before churn, and webFamilyPlanPricing already resolved $159.99 as the winner on web.

The invite did not work, but the completion-rate comparison is not what proves it. At n=57 the 54.8% versus 73.1% gap reaches only about 85% confidence - underpowered, and we would not call a paywall test on that margin. What is decisive is the direct funnel measurement: of the 17 users who actually saw the hosted 2-minute survey invite, 2 accepted it. An 11.8% acceptance rate is a product fact rather than a statistical inference, and no sample size would rescue a screen that 15 of 17 people dismiss. The invite also added a dismissal step to a flow whose entire purpose is a single question, which is the most plausible reading of the directional drop in completion. Control shipped. Recorded here with the underpowered caveat explicit so a future reader does not cite the 54.8%/73.1% delta as a significant result. Move the invite off the completion path. Hypothesis: the invite suppresses completion because it interrupts it - show it only after the modal completes, or a day later by push or email. Variants: a: post-completion invite, b: day-later push, c: control. Primary metric: survey acceptance rate; guardrail: Helpfulness Modal Completion Rate.

Power the surface before reading it again. Not a growth test - test design. 57 assigned users in 12 days means any future variant on the helpfulness modal needs roughly 6-8 weeks, or a wider trigger, to separate a 15-point completion difference. Decide the minimum detectable effect before launching rather than reading an 85% result afterwards.
